analysis.investment_thesis: Exim Routes is a 6-year-old commodity paper trading intermediary with zero operating cash generation (0/5 years positive OCF) despite reporting ₹8 Cr net profit, signalling poor earnings quality. At 37.5x P/E on a low-moat, capital-consumptive trading business, this is structurally unattractive and severely overpriced.
key_strengths: High reported ROE (54%) and ROCE (55.3%), though inflated by tiny equity base of ₹25 Cr
Revenue scale-up from ₹4 Cr to ₹121 Cr in 4 years shows execution momentum in sourcing recyclable paper
Some institutional interest (FII 7.55%, DII 6.32%) lends marginal credibility
key_risks: Negative OCF every single year — ₹8 Cr net profit in 2025 yet OCF was -₹5 Cr, FCF was -₹9 Cr; profits are not real cash
Zero economic moat — paper material trading is purely commoditised with no pricing power, brand, or switching costs
P/E of 37.5x is nearly double my ceiling for a quality business, and this is not a quality business — it's a commodity middleman
red_flags: Profits never converted to cash in 5 years — severe working capital deterioration or earnings manipulation risk
Debt growing from ₹1 Cr (2021) to ₹9 Cr (2025) while OCF stays negative — debt is funding operating losses
Company incorporated April 2019 — no business cycle test, no recession experience, no dividend history
134.5% revenue CAGR is speculative explosion, not the steady 10-15% CAGR I demand — unsustainable and usually mean-reverts badly
Promoter at 52.44% — below my 55% minimum, and no data on trajectory
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Exim Routes is exactly the type of business I have learned to avoid over decades: a commodity trading intermediary with no brand, no pricing power, and no repeat-purchase loyalty. Paper recycling is a volume game dominated by whoever can offer the lowest spread. The reported ROE of 54% on a ₹25 Cr equity base sounds exciting but is meaningless when the business has never generated a single rupee of positive operating cash flow. In 2025, the company reported ₹8 Cr net profit yet burned ₹5 Cr in operations and ₹4 Cr in investing — financed entirely by ₹11 Cr from debt and equity raises. This is not a business making money; it is a business consuming money while accounting shows a profit.

At ₹248 Cr market cap and 37.5x P/E, the market is pricing this as though it is a franchise business. It is not. It is a 6-year-old startup trading in recyclable paper with ₹54 Cr in total assets. I built DMart by waiting for businesses with proven, cash-generative models before paying a price. This stock fails every filter I apply: no positive cash flow, no moat, no dividend, no track record through a downturn, and a valuation suited for a compounding franchise. I would not invest a single rupee here.
